sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Árgos** (*argos*) — The All-Seeing · Hera's Hundred-Eyed Watcher — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Vigilance, Hera's Watcher". The name means "Shining, swift"[^1].

Árgos Panoptes is the perfect sentinel of Greek myth: a giant whose body was set with eyes that slept only in relays, so that some were always open. Hera chose him to guard the cow that had been Io. He is the myth's meditation on watchfulness — its power, its cost, and its strange afterlife in feathers.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Árgos** and serves its temple at [árgos.com](https://xn--rgos-4na.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *argos* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Ἄργος**. Etymologically it means "Shining, swift"[^1].

The ASCII form *argos* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Árgos** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **Á** — Acute on a
- **r** → **r** — r same
- **g** → **g** — g same
- **o** → **o** — o same
- **s** → **s** — s same

The project holds the domain **árgos.com** (xn--rgos-4na.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ár.gos/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Á-** — Alpha with acute pitch [á] — a bright, open attack; the whole name flashes on its first syllable.
- **-r-** — Rolled alveolar rho [r] — the quick turn at the name's center.
- **-gos** — Voiced velar gamma with short omicron and final sigma [gos] — clipped, unlenited, watchful.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'AR-goss' — two short syllables, stress forward, like a light snapping on.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek adjective** — ἀργός, 'shining, white, gleaming' — and, by the flash of motion, 'swift'
- **Greek noun** — ἄργυρος, 'silver', from the same root
- **PIE** — *h₂erǵ-, 'white, shining', whence also Latin argentum
- **Epithet** — Πανόπτης (Panoptēs), 'the All-Seeing', his fixed title in the myth

Árgos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄργος carries only the acute stress; both vowels are short, so a single feature separates the restoration from ASCII. The name belongs to the giant Argos Panoptes, Hera's watcher — not to the city of the Argolid, though the two share the shining root.

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Loeb Classical Library (Frazer), 150.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Árgos Panoptes is the perfect sentinel of Greek myth: a giant whose body was set with eyes that slept only in relays, so that some were always open. Hera chose him to guard the cow that had been Io. He is the myth's meditation on watchfulness — its power, its cost, and its strange afterlife in feathers.[^1]

### The Hundred Eyes

Ovid gives him a hundred eyes ringed about his head; the tragedians make him many-eyed, and later art covers his whole body with them. Two slept while the others watched.

### Hera's Guard

Chosen by the queen of heaven herself to watch Io — the one servant whose vigilance could be trusted absolutely.

### The Sleepless Watch

His eyes took turns at rest; there was no hour, no dusk, no dawn in which the prisoner was unseen.

### The Peacock's Tail

Slain by Hermês, he was memorialized by his mistress: Hera set his eyes on the tail of her bird, where they watch still.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Árgos concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The hundred eyes** — Vigilance that never wholly sleeps
- **The peacock** — Hera's bird; the eyes on its tail are his memorial
- **The white cow** — Io transformed, the charge he was set to guard
- **The herdsman's staff** — His gear as a common cowherd on the roads of the Argolid
- **The curved sword** — The harpē of Hermês, by which the watcher was finally put to sleep

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Loeb Classical Library (Frazer), 150.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Árgos exists within a single great story — the wanderings of Io — but it is one of the oldest stories the Greeks told, already old when Homer gave Hermês the epithet **Argeiphontēs, 'Slayer of Árgos'**.[^1]

### Hera Sets the Watch (The Appointment)

Zeús loved Io, daughter of the river-god Inachos, and to hide her from Hera — so the common telling runs — she was changed into a white cow. Hera was not deceived. She asked for the cow as a gift, and set over it Árgos Panoptes, the all-seeing giant, who tethered his prisoner to an olive tree in the grove of Mycenae and watched her without rest.[^2]

### The Herdsman Who Never Sleeps (The Watch)

Árgos kept Io as a cowherd keeps a beast: by day she grazed under his eyes, by night she was bound. The poets dwell on the horror of it — a princess eating grass, a guard with nowhere to look away. Aeschylus makes him the many-eyed herdsman whose vigil not even the earth could bury.

### Hermês Argeiphontēs (The Slaying)

Zeús sent Hermês to end it. Disguised as a shepherd, the god played the syrinx and told, in Ovid's account, the very story of how the pipes were made — the tale of Syrinx — until one by one the hundred eyes grew heavy and closed. Then Hermês drew the curved sword and struck off the watcher's head. The epithet Argeiphontēs, 'Slayer of Árgos', clung to him forever after.

### The Eyes on the Peacock (The Memorial)

Hera took the eyes of her dead servant and set them in the tail of her peacock, where they gleam like jewels. But she did not forgive the prisoner: she sent a gadfly to sting Io into madness and drive her over the world — past the Bosporos, the 'cow's crossing' that bears her name still, to Egypt, where Zeús restored her with a touch.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Árgos never became a god and was never identified with foreign deities; his afterlife is in the natural world and in language. Rome kept him as Argus — Ovid's account in the Metamorphoses is the fullest surviving version — and made the transfer of his eyes the aition, the explanatory myth, of the peacock's plumage. Later readers saw in his hundred eyes the starry sky itself, set as heaven's watchman over the world. His name also lives disguised in Hermês's oldest epithet: Argeiphontēs appears already in the Iliad, proof that the story of the slain watcher was archaic before Homer sang.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Loeb Classical Library (Frazer), 150.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: English keeps him in the phrase 'argus-eyed', watchful beyond fatigue. Newspapers across the English-speaking world took the name The Argus — the all-seeing press — and naturalists gave it to the argus pheasant, whose feathers are spotted with eyes in exact obedience to the myth. Every camera grid and sensor network re-enacts him: Árgos is the mythic ancestor of all surveillance, and his fate is its parable. The watcher who saw everything was undone by music and a story — the oldest recorded defeat of total vigilance by art.[^1]

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Loeb Classical Library (Frazer), 150.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Árgos Panoptes had no cult and no temple; the Greeks themselves knew him as a figure of the primeval Argolid, and his material presence is pictorial. Attic and South Italian vases of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE show him exactly as the poets describe — a herdsman whose body is seeded with eyes, standing guard over the cow Io, or falling beneath Hermês's sword. His landscape survives: the Heraion of Argos, the great sanctuary of his mistress, and the olive grove of Mycenae where the sources place his watch. The myth's honesty is part of its interest — the all-seeing watcher left nothing behind but pictures of his own watching.[^1]

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Loeb Classical Library (Frazer), 150.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
There is a peculiar pathos in Árgos. He is the one figure in the Io story without desire: Zeús wants, Hera rages, Io suffers, but Árgos only watches. He is duty itself, a creature made of attention. The myth does not call him wicked; Hera's grief for him is real, and his memorial is beautiful. Yet the story knows that perfect vigilance is a kind of death-in-life — a mind with no interior, no sleep, no dream.

And so the manner of his fall matters. He is not overpowered; no hero wrestles him down. He is lulled — by music, and by a story about the music. The hundred eyes close one after another, like lamps in a city at midnight, and in the last of them the sword is already falling. It is the most civilized killing in Greek myth, and the most ominous: attention can be sung to sleep. Hera could preserve his eyes, but not his seeing. The peacock's tail is the most gorgeous surveillance apparatus in the world, and it watches nothing at all.[^1]
